source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Corn reaches physiological maturity when grain moisture content is around 30-32%, but farmers should wait to harvest until grain moisture has dropped to roughly 18-24%. Since most farmers do not own a grain moisture meter, they must judge maturity by other visual signs, described below.

Color-based maturity signs (which vary by variety and season): In the early wet season (roughly March-July), the stalk and upper leaves remain green while the lower leaves and the husk turn a pale straw-yellow. In the late wet season (roughly July-December), the entire plant — stalk, leaves, and husk — dies back and turns pale straw-yellow.

Kernel-based maturity signs: mature kernels are hard, glossy/shiny, and develop a dark (black) abscission layer. In some varieties, the ear also droops downward when mature.

Harvest timing should follow the maturity period (days to maturity) recommended by the seed company for the specific variety, in order to avoid two problems: over-mature grain increases the rate of kernel breakage/cracking during milling; and rain falling on an over-mature, standing crop can cause discoloration, mold/fungal growth, or premature sprouting on the ear — this is a particular risk for varieties whose husk does not fully close over/cover the cob.

Field examples recorded from Pailin farmers: farmers harvesting in the early wet season typically harvest at around 29% grain moisture, while farmers harvesting in the late wet season typically harvest at around 21% grain moisture.
